items.title: Dave Brubeck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Wilton, Connecticut, November 21, 2001

ctx.x: Yeah. Yesterday we found out we’re not doing my Easter cantata in Vienna, which was very disappointing to Russell Gloyd, our conductor, but he said, “well then we’ll record it with the London Symphony Orchestra.” I’m trying to make up my mind whether to do the Easter cantata, which is called “Beloved Son” or “Tongues of Fire,” which is about after Christ comes back and fire descends on the disciples and they all speak in tongues and everything. That’s a very different kind of cantata. And I think it’s only been…

A recent quote that you had about a CD of yours called “The Crossing,” you said it’s so important to have this message of freedom going all over the world, prophetic I think, even more important these days I think.

items.title: Dave Brubeck — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Russell has had one rehearsal with the choir and the musicians.

ctx.x: So we’re on the way to Japan or Australia, and I said, “If I show the director of the choir, and he’s the person that’s going to be working with this – have him come to the airport in San Francisco and meet us. We’ll go to some room, and I’ll show him the music that I’ve started.” So he meets us there, and I said, “I think I’ve found the solution. I think I’ve written a fugue.” He said, “Let me see it.” He looks at it and sings perfectly the subject, then the counter-subject, then the stretto. “What do you mean,…

said, “I can defend this music. I’m a musician.” So we get to the part – now I’ve got the quartet. Russell has had one rehearsal with the choir and the musicians. I wrote it for 21 brass and percussion, because outdoors, in a baseball diamond – the altar is on second base, put up like a jigsaw puzzle, just perfectly, very expensive, because they’ve got to put it up and take it down, because there’s a ball game there that night. Can you imagine? It cost hundreds of thousands of dollars. I forget exactly. So [ ]…
